nodeData.note: What soil and plant microbiology has learned since 2020, explained for farmers and field teams. Each bubble says how mature the idea is and links the paper behind it.

children.note: New DNA tools let scientists see which microbes live in and around crops and what they do. This is changing how biofertilizers and biopesticides are designed.
Older products used a single microbe. New research studies whole communities of microbes that work together, because single strains often fail to settle in field soil.

children.topic: Lab results are not field results
children.note: Many striking results come from pots or sterile soil. Benefits usually shrink in real fields, so treat new claims as promising until local trials confirm them.

manas.q: Why should a farmer be careful with results from pot or lab trials?

children.note: Maturity tags: LAB = only in laboratory or greenhouse; FIELD TRIALS = tested in farms by researchers; MARKET = products sold. 📄 bubbles link the paper.
The rhizosphere is the thin layer of soil around roots. Research since 2020 shows plants actively shape who lives there.

A global analysis of 557 soil pairs found the rhizosphere holds fewer kinds of bacteria than bulk soil: roots select a subset. Genes for N fixation were enriched near roots and nitrification genes depleted.

manas.q: Is the rhizosphere more or less diverse than bulk soil, and why?

children.note: Roots leak sugars, acids and special compounds. These feed chosen microbes and send chemical signals, making the root zone a hotspot of activity.
When attacked or stressed, plants change their exudates and attract helpful microbes. Proving that this shift actually benefits the plant is still hard.

manas.q: What is the plant 'cry for help'?

children.note: In model plants, the phosphate-starvation response also changes root immunity and the root microbiome, linking plant nutrition and microbe recruitment.
Living roots for more months of the year, crop diversity and organic matter give roots more to offer microbes. Maturity: principle well supported; exact recipes still FIELD TRIALS.
Scientists look for the 'core' microbes always found with a crop, then build small designed communities (SynComs) from them.
The set of microbes found consistently with a crop across many soils and seasons. They are thought to do key jobs and to fit that plant well.

manas.q: What is a crop's core microbiome?

children.note: A 2024 study found SynComs built from native core microbes supported plant growth better than non-native ones, and helped resident beneficial microbes settle. This was a pot study.
A synthetic community is a small mix of chosen strains, picked to work together. New designs choose strains by function (what genes they carry), not only by name.

manas.q: What is a SynCom?

children.note: A Bacillus velezensis inoculant fed and boosted a native Pseudomonas in cucumber roots. Products may work partly by waking up local microbes.
SynComs are mostly LAB and greenhouse work; a few multi-strain products are in FIELD TRIALS. Expect variable results across soils.
Cereals like maize, wheat and rice cannot form root nodules, so researchers are looking for other ways to get them fixed nitrogen.
Legumes have a special signalling pathway to host Rhizobium in nodules. Cereals do not, so N-fixers can only live on or inside them loosely.

manas.q: Why can't maize host nitrogen-fixing nodules like beans?

children.note: An old maize landrace from Oaxaca, Mexico grows aerial roots that drip sugary mucilage full of N-fixing bacteria. Over 5 years, fixation supplied 29–82% of its nitrogen.

manas.q: What did the Sierra Mixe maize study find?

children.note: Maize xylem sap holds a stable core of bacteria, many with nitrogenase genes. A 4-strain SynCom supplied about 12% of stem N in tests.
Bacteria such as Azospirillum and Azotobacter add some N in cereal fields, but legumes in rotation remain the largest biological N source.
Long-term projects try to give cereals nodule-like abilities or engineer their microbes. Maturity: LAB; not expected on farms soon.
Gene-edited soil bacteria that keep fixing N even in fertilised fields are sold for maize in the USA (see New Technologies map). Not allowed in organic farming.
Some plants release root compounds that slow nitrifying microbes, so nitrogen stays as ammonium longer and less is lost.
Nitrifying microbes turn ammonium into nitrate, which leaches or becomes nitrous oxide gas. BNI plants exude natural inhibitors that slow this step.

manas.q: What does biological nitrification inhibition do to soil nitrogen?

children.note: The tropical forage grass Brachiaria humidicola releases brachialactone, which gave 60–90% of its root inhibition activity.

manas.q: Which compound gives Brachiaria its BNI effect?

children.note: A chromosome piece from wild grass Leymus racemosus was bred into elite wheat, roughly doubling BNI and cutting soil nitrifier activity and N2O. Maturity: FIELD TRIALS.

manas.q: How was BNI-wheat created?

children.note: Sorghum roots exude sorgoleone, a compound linked to BNI. A 2021 study showed it also reshapes soil bacterial communities.
Drought-tolerant and sensitive pearl millet lines exuded different compounds with different BNI activity, so BNI varies by variety and stress.

links.label: 📄 Source: Biology and Fertility of Soils 2022

children.note: In a two-season field trial, Brachiaria sown with maize did not reduce maize yield and recycled about 140 kg N/ha in its biomass after harvest. A practical way to use BNI plants today.
BNI favours an ammonium-based N economy with less leaching. Brachiaria forages are already on MARKET; BNI cereals are still FIELD TRIALS.
Fungal threads can link the roots of several plants. What these links really do in fields and forests is now debated.
A common mycorrhizal network forms when fungal hyphae connect roots of two or more plants, of the same or different species.

manas.q: What is a common mycorrhizal network?

children.note: Mycorrhizal fungi improve plant access to phosphorus, nitrogen and water in exchange for plant carbon. This is well established.

links.label: 📄 Source: Annual Review of Plant Biology 2023

children.note: A 2024 meta-analysis found AM fungi raised plant biomass on average, but effects were larger in lab than in field trials and larger with legumes.
A 2023 review found that claims about networks being widespread and moving resources to help seedlings are weakly supported by field evidence.

manas.q: What did the 2023 review conclude about the 'wood wide web'?

children.note: The same review found no peer-reviewed evidence that mature trees send resources or warnings to their offspring through fungal networks.
Protect native fungi anyway: less tillage, moderate phosphorus, living roots and cover crops. Do not buy products sold on 'plants talk' stories.
In some soils a disease stays low even when the pathogen and a susceptible crop are present. Microbes are a big part of the reason.

General suppression comes from lots of active microbes competing with pathogens. Specific suppression comes from particular microbes acting against one pathogen and can be transferred with small amounts of soil.

manas.q: What is the difference between general and specific disease suppression?

links.label: 📄 Source: J. Soil Sci. Plant Nutrition 2021

children.note: When a fungus attacked sugar beet roots, endophytic bacteria inside the root increased and made antifungal compounds; a small consortium of two of these bacterial groups suppressed the disease.

manas.q: What did the 2019 sugar beet endophyte study show?

children.note: Harmless derivatives of a pathogen made plants assemble a disease-suppressing root microbiome in a 2024 study. Maturity: LAB.
Organic matter, compost, crop rotation and cover crops tend to raise general suppression. Specific suppression is harder to create on purpose.

links.label: 📄 Source: J. Soil Sci. Plant Nutrition 2021

children.note: Much of the long-lasting carbon in soil turns out to be the remains of dead microbes, not just plant residues.
Necromass is the dead bodies and cell walls of bacteria and fungi. Some of it binds to clay and silt and can stay in soil for a long time.

manas.q: What is microbial necromass?

children.topic: More than half of soil carbon
children.note: A global analysis of biomarker data suggested microbial necromass can make up more than half of topsoil organic carbon in farmland, grassland and forest.

manas.q: Roughly how much soil organic carbon can come from microbial necromass?

children.note: Carbon stuck to soil minerals is the most stable kind. A 2022 study mapped how much more of it soils could hold worldwide.
More plant species led to faster microbial growth and turnover and more soil carbon in a long grassland experiment.
Across four climate zones, paddy soils stored organic carbon more efficiently than nearby upland soils, through different pathways.
Feed microbes steadily with roots, residues, compost and diverse crops; their remains build lasting carbon. Maturity: science solid, carbon-credit measurement still hard.
The phyllosphere is the above-ground surface of plants, mainly leaves, home to bacteria, yeasts and fungi.
Leaf microbes face sun, drying and few nutrients. Some protect plants by competing with pathogens or triggering plant defences.

manas.q: What is the phyllosphere?

children.note: Warming, drought, higher CO2 and pollution change leaf microbial communities and their links with the plant, a 2022 review found.
Microbes sprayed on leaves face UV and drying, so timing (evening, humid weather) and good formulation matter. Maturity: MARKET for some biocontrols.
Heat, drought and floods change both crops and their microbes, and shift where diseases occur.
A 2022 review proposed that in the short term (years to decades) the microbiome drives much of plant adaptation to climate change.

manas.q: According to a 2022 review, what drives plant adaptation to climate change in the short term?

children.note: Warming changes where pathogens can live, how fast they evolve and how severe outbreaks are, threatening food security.

manas.q: How does climate change affect plant diseases?

children.note: Under drought, links between soil bacteria and fungi changed more than simple species counts showed.
Floods cut oxygen to roots and change which microbes thrive; some help plants cope, others are pathogens.
A meta-analysis of 57 studies found PGPR inoculation improved many plant traits under drought, mostly in controlled experiments.
Much remains open. Knowing the gaps helps teams avoid overselling.
The same inoculant may work in one soil and fail in the next. Soil type, native microbes, weather and crop variety all matter.

manas.q: Name three reasons an inoculant may work in one field but not another.

children.note: Many added microbes decline within weeks. How to help them colonise roots is a major research question.
Most soil microbes have never been grown in a lab, so their roles are guessed from DNA.

children.topic: Yield and profit data are thin
children.note: Few long-term, farm-scale trials in Africa and India measure yield and income from new biologicals.
Where this research touches East Africa and South Asia.
Brachiaria forages are grown in Kenya for livestock and as a border crop in push-pull systems; their BNI is a bonus for nitrogen.
Sorghum and pearl millet, key Indian dryland crops, are being screened for BNI; the drought study shows variety choice matters.

links.label: 📄 Source: Biology and Fertility of Soils 2022

children.note: New strains need registration: PCPB/KEPHIS in Kenya, FCO (biofertilizers) or CIB&RC (biopesticides) in India. Gene-edited microbes face extra rules.
Talks and short films on the research above.

children.topic: ▶ This slime could change the world
children.note: BBC Earth Science: the Mexican maize with N-fixing aerial-root slime.
Prof. Corné Pieterse (Tohoku University lecture): how roots recruit helpful microbes.
Prof. Philip Poole (Gatsby Plant Science): rhizosphere bacteria and N fixation.
Crowther Lab: mapping mycorrhizal fungi worldwide.

children.topic: ▶ Justine Karst: wood wide web truth
children.note: Long interview with an author of the 2023 review on what the evidence shows.
Background reading.
Overview of microbes living on and in plants.
The root zone and its chemistry and biology.
Common networks and the current debate.
Types and mechanisms of suppressive soils.

nodeData.note: New tools for biological and organic farming: smarter inoculants, better formulations, nano and RNA products, pheromones, drones, DNA tests, digital soil maps and AI apps. Each bubble gives maturity, access in Kenya and India, and cautions.

children.topic: How to judge a new technology
children.note: A short checklist before spending money or recommending a product.
LAB = works in a laboratory; FIELD TRIALS = tested on farms by researchers; MARKET = sold. Many 'new' products are sold before strong field data exist.

manas.q: What are the three maturity stages used in this map?

children.note: Ask for replicated trials in your region, crop and soil, with an untreated control. Testimonials and pot photos are not enough.
Organic standards (NPOP in India, East African Organic Products Standard, EU, USDA) exclude genetically engineered organisms and synthetic fertilisers. Confirm with your certifier.

manas.q: Which two kinds of input are excluded by organic standards regardless of how new they are?

children.note: Kenya: PCPB registers biopesticides, KEPHIS handles plant health and imports. India: FCO covers biofertilizers and nano fertilizers; CIB&RC registers biopesticides.
Inoculants are moving from single strains to mixtures, inside-the-plant microbes and edited strains.
Products combine several microbes, such as N-fixers, P-solubilisers and K-mobilisers, in one pack. Maturity: MARKET in India and Kenya.

manas.q: What is a microbial consortium product?

children.note: Endophytes live inside plant tissues, where they are protected from soil competition. Products based on them are emerging. Maturity: FIELD TRIALS to early MARKET.
Soil bacteria are gene-edited so their N-fixation 'off switch' no longer works in fertilised soil. One strain fixed 122 times more N in N-rich conditions than its parent.

manas.q: What change is made in remodelled nitrogen-fixing bacteria?

children.note: Sold for maize in the USA as seed or in-furrow treatments, supplying part of the crop's N. Not registered in Kenya or India as far as we know.
Gene-edited microbes count as genetic engineering, an excluded method in organic standards. Do not use them on certified farms.

manas.q: Can gene-edited N-fixing microbes be used on certified organic farms?

children.note: Inoculants supply only part of crop N and need living roots and moisture. Many added strains decline in soil within weeks.
How microbes are packed decides whether they arrive alive. Formulation is where much recent progress has been made.
Microbes are trapped in beads or capsules of alginate, chitosan, gums or starch that protect them and release them slowly. Maturity: FIELD TRIALS, some MARKET.

manas.q: Name two materials used to encapsulate microbes.

children.note: Chitosan, made from crustacean shells, can carry microbes and also triggers plant defences; its effect depends on molecular weight.
Microbes are coated on seed with stickers and protectants at the factory, so the farmer plants treated seed. Survival on stored seed is the main challenge.
Liquids with protective additives are easy to use in drip and sprayers and often keep longer than carrier powders. Store cool and out of sun.
Liquid biofertilizers are widely sold in India; encapsulated and pre-coated seed are still rare and cost more in both countries.
Fertilisers made as tiny particles, claimed to be absorbed better so much less is needed.
Nutrients such as N, Zn or Cu prepared as particles smaller than 100 nanometres, usually sprayed on leaves.

manas.q: What is a nano-fertilizer?

children.note: Plant scientists warn that many nano-agriculture papers ignore basic plant and soil science, and that claimed savings are often not proven.

manas.q: Why are scientists cautious about nano-fertilizer claims?

children.note: A 2025 review explains that particles entering leaves and moving through the plant face strong barriers, limiting how much nutrient they deliver.
Long-term effects of nanoparticles on soil life, water and people are poorly known; silver nanoparticles, for example, are toxic to microbes.
India added nano fertilizers to the FCO and they are sold nationwide. Synthetic nano fertilizers are not allowed in organic farming.

manas.q: Are synthetic nano fertilizers allowed in organic farming?

children.note: MARKET in India; FIELD TRIALS elsewhere. Do not replace soil fertility plans with nano sprays; test on a small plot first.
Sprays of double-stranded RNA that silence a vital gene in one pest or pathogen.
dsRNA matching a pest gene is sprayed on leaves. When the pest eats it, its own RNAi machinery shuts that gene down and the pest dies.

manas.q: How does a dsRNA spray kill a pest?

children.note: Ledprona targets Colorado potato beetle and was approved by the US EPA in 2023. In lab tests a tiny dose killed 90% of larvae.

manas.q: What was the first sprayable dsRNA insecticide aimed at?

children.note: Loading dsRNA on clay nanosheets (BioClay) extended protection against grey mould on tomato leaves from about 1 to 3 weeks.
RNA breaks down fast outdoors. Sap-sucking insects and fungi inside tissue are hard to reach because sprayed RNA moves poorly into plants.
Very specific to the target species, but regulators still assess off-target effects and persistence.
No dsRNA spray is known to be registered in Kenya or India yet. Not on organic input lists; check with your certifier.
Insect scent signals used to monitor or confuse pests. They are among the most farmer-ready tools here.
Pheromone traps catch males of one species, showing when a pest arrives and how many. Used for fall armyworm, fruit flies and bollworms.

manas.q: What do pheromone traps mainly tell a farmer?

children.note: Many dispensers flood the crop with female scent so males cannot find mates. Passive dispensers are placed at 200–3000 per hectare.

manas.q: How does mating disruption work?

children.note: Timed aerosol devices release pheromone from fewer points, saving labour, though placement and dose need care.
Repellent intercrops push pests away and attractive border grasses pull them out. Developed by icipe in Kenya for maize stemborers and fall armyworm.
Pheromones in traps and dispensers are allowed in organic farming, as they do not touch the food.
Works best over large areas and at low pest numbers. Traps for one species do not control others.
Drones spray liquids or drop beneficial insects over fields, reaching difficult terrain fast.
Drones apply low volumes of liquid, which is a challenge for live microbes: fine droplets dry fast and UV harms them. Spray early or late.
Drones release Trichogramma egg parasitoids and predatory mites over crops. Maturity: MARKET in Europe and China, early elsewhere.
India has drone rules and spraying procedures for agriculture; in Kenya operators need KCAA licensing. Use certified pilots.
Usually hired per acre from service providers. Large-scale fields benefit most; small plots are often cheaper by hand.
Labs sequence DNA in soil samples to list which microbes are present.
Amplicon sequencing reads one marker gene to name bacteria or fungi; metagenomics reads all DNA to estimate functions as well.

manas.q: What is the difference between amplicon sequencing and metagenomics?

children.note: DNA shows who is present, not who is active. There are no agreed thresholds yet linking test results to fertiliser or yield advice.

manas.q: Why can a soil DNA test not tell you if microbes are active?

children.note: Mainly sold in the USA and Europe; in Kenya and India mostly research labs. Costs more than a standard soil test.
Use a standard soil test, slake test, infiltration and earthworm counts first. Add DNA tests for research or long trials.
Computer models combine soil samples and satellite data to predict soil properties everywhere.
Africa-wide maps of pH, organic carbon, N, P, K, micronutrients and texture at 30 m pixels and three depths, made with machine learning.

manas.q: What resolution does the iSDAsoil Africa map have?

children.note: iSDAsoil is free online, and similar national data support fertiliser and lime advice in Kenya.
India's Soil Health Card scheme gives farmers lab soil test results with nutrient advice; digital maps add a wider view.
Maps are predictions with errors and may miss field-to-field differences. Confirm with your own soil test before big decisions.
Measuring soil carbon cheaply matters for soil health tracking and carbon credits.
Satellite images with machine learning estimate topsoil carbon over large areas, best on bare soil.
Labs scan dried soil with infrared light and predict carbon and other properties quickly and cheaply after calibration with chemistry tests.
Soil carbon credits face problems with measurement, permanence and fairness to farmers, a 2023 review warns.

manas.q: Name one problem with soil carbon certificates.

children.note: Phone apps that recognise crop problems from photos of leaves.
Free app from Penn State, FAO, IITA, CIMMYT and partners that diagnoses crop problems on the phone without internet.
For cassava diseases in East Africa, Nuru was right 65% of the time, more than extension agents (40–58%) and farmers (18–31%).

manas.q: How did Nuru's accuracy compare with extension agents in cassava tests?

children.note: Photograph clear symptoms on several plants, check the advice with an expert and confirm with a lab when stakes are high.
Apps cover a limited list of crops and diseases and can miss nutrient problems or new pests.
Charcoal made by heating biomass with little air, used as a soil conditioner.
A stable, porous carbon made by pyrolysis of crop waste or wood. It can hold water and nutrients and lasts long in soil.

manas.q: How is biochar made?

children.note: A 2022 meta-analysis of 57 studies found biochar raised yields on average, with the biggest gains in very acidic soils (pH 5 or below).

manas.q: On what kind of soil does biochar raise yields most?

links.label: 📄 Source: Science of the Total Environment 2022

children.note: Fresh biochar can hold nutrients away from plants. Mix with compost, manure or urine first so it is 'charged'.
Biochar locks carbon for a long time, and accounting models exist to count it.
Usually accepted in organic farming if made from untreated plant material; check your certifier. Avoid char from treated wood or plastics.
Made on farm with simple kilns in Kenya and India; bagged products cost more. Many carbon projects now pay for biochar.
Short videos on these technologies.
iSDA team explains how the 30 m Africa soil maps were made.
PlantVillage: a Kenyan farmer shows how to download and use Nuru.
Nature Video animation of how RNAi silences genes.
Rothamsted Research on pheromone-based pest control.
Citizen TV Kenya (Smart Farm): farmers making and using biochar.
EMBL: how DNA from a whole sample is sequenced and analysed.
Background reading.
How pheromones confuse pest insects.
The icipe push-pull system.
How soil maps are predicted.
Production, uses and evidence.

nodeData.note: Key discoveries, pioneers, success stories and failures that shaped biological and organic farming worldwide, with evidence links. Use it to learn what has worked, where, and why.

children.note: In about fifty years, scientists showed that invisible microbes feed plants, recycle nutrients and fight disease. Almost every biological input sold today traces back to these discoveries.

German agricultural chemists Hermann Hellriegel and Hermann Wilfarth showed that legumes take nitrogen from the air only when their root nodules are present. They reported it in 1886 and published fully in 1888.

manas.q: Who first showed that legume nodules let plants use nitrogen from the air, and when?

children.note: Dutch microbiologist Martinus Beijerinck grew the nodule bacteria in pure culture, the organisms later named Rhizobium. This made it possible to multiply them and put them in a packet.
In 1901 Beijerinck showed that Azotobacter chroococcum fixes nitrogen while living freely in soil, without any plant partner. It is still a common biofertiliser.

Sergei Winogradsky identified the nitrifying bacteria (Nitrosomonas, Nitrobacter) that turn ammonium into nitrate, and Clostridium pasteurianum, an anaerobic free-living nitrogen fixer. He founded soil microbial ecology.
German botanist Albert Bernhard Frank coined the word mycorrhiza ('fungus-root') in 1885, while studying how fungi on tree roots feed the trees.

manas.q: Who coined the word 'mycorrhiza', and in which year?

children.note: Only ten years after the nodule discovery, the first commercially produced rhizobial inoculant, Nitragin, appeared in 1896. Inoculants are among the oldest biological products in farming.

manas.q: When did the first commercial rhizobial inoculant appear?

links.label: 📄 Source: Santos et al. 2019, AMB Express (inoculant history review)

children.note: In 1932 Weindling described Trichoderma coiling around and parasitising other fungi such as Rhizoctonia. This mycoparasitism is the basis of today's Trichoderma biofungicides.

manas.q: What did Weindling observe about Trichoderma in 1932?

links.label: 📄 Source: Schuster & Schmoll 2010, Appl Microbiol Biotechnol

children.note: Bacillus thuringiensis was first found in sick silkworms in Japan (1901) and rediscovered by Berliner in German flour-moth caterpillars (1911). Bt sprays were on sale in France by the late 1930s.
The organic movement grew in the 1920s–1970s as a reaction to soil decline and the rise of chemical farming. Many of its ideas came from Indian and East Asian peasant practice.
Eight lectures on agriculture in 1924 started biodynamic farming. Its compost preparations are popular, but its cosmic elements are not supported by science.

children.topic: Albert Howard and the Indore method
children.note: British botanist Albert Howard worked at Indore, India, and turned local composting practice into the Indore method. He called Indian farmers and pests his 'professors'.

manas.q: In which country did Albert Howard develop the Indore composting method?

children.note: Howard's 1940 book argued that soil health, plant health and human health are one chain, built on returning organic matter to the soil. It remains a classic organic text.
Publisher J. I. Rodale popularised organic gardening and farming in America through magazines and books, and founded what became the Rodale Institute.
Japanese farmer-philosopher Masanobu Fukuoka (1913–2008) practised no-till, no-herbicide, no-pesticide natural farming and seed balls. His ideas influenced natural farming in India.

manas.q: Which Japanese farmer is known for 'do-nothing' natural farming?

children.note: The International Federation of Organic Agriculture Movements, founded in 1972, set the shared principles on which most national organic standards are built.
Synthetic nitrogen and new seed varieties raised yields enormously from the 1910s to the 1970s. They also created the soil, water and cost problems that biological farming now tries to fix.
Fritz Haber made ammonia from air in 1909; Carl Bosch scaled it up at BASF, with the first factory running in 1913. Both won Nobel Prizes.

manas.q: When did the first industrial Haber–Bosch ammonia plant start?

children.note: Factory nitrogen now feeds a large share of humanity. But it needs fossil energy, and much of the nitrogen leaks to water and air instead of reaching the crop.

links.label: 📄 Source: Gu et al. 2023, Nature (cropland N pollution)

children.note: High-yielding wheat and rice, irrigation, fertiliser and pesticides lifted yields in Mexico, India and Asia. Norman Borlaug received the 1970 Nobel Peace Prize.
In India and elsewhere the gains came with declining soil organic matter, groundwater depletion, nutrient imbalances and a narrower diet. These lessons drive today's interest in soil biology.

links.label: 📄 Source: Front. Sustain. Food Syst. 2021, Green Revolution lessons

children.topic: Bt today: spray yes, GM crop no
children.note: Bt sprays made from the bacterium are allowed in organic farming. Bt crops, which carry Bt genes, are genetically modified and are NOT allowed in organic certification.

manas.q: Are Bt sprays and Bt (GM) crops both allowed in organic farming?

children.note: Brazil grows one of the world's largest soybean crops relying mainly on Bradyrhizobium inoculants instead of nitrogen fertiliser. It is the biggest biological-input success story.
Soybean seed is inoculated with selected Bradyrhizobium strains (e.g. SEMIA 5079 and 5080) and the crop normally receives no nitrogen fertiliser. Research by Embrapa backed this from the 1960s on.

links.label: 📄 Source: Brazil J. Microbiol. 2019, inoculant quality

children.topic: About US$20 billion saved per year
children.note: A 2019 review estimates that growing soybean without nitrogen fertiliser saves Brazil roughly US$20 billion a year.

manas.q: Roughly how much does Brazil save per year by growing soybean on inoculants instead of N fertiliser?

links.label: 📄 Source: Santos et al. 2019, AMB Express (inoculant history review)

children.note: Brazilian rules set minimum counts; most liquid products tested in 2010–2014 guaranteed around 5 × 10⁹ CFU/ml and only about 2% had contaminants. Quality kept farmers' trust.

links.label: 📄 Source: Brazil J. Microbiol. 2019, inoculant quality

children.note: Adding Azospirillum to Bradyrhizobium raised soybean yield by about 3.2% on average across Brazilian trials (2009–2020), with more benefit on sandy soils and under stress.
Success came from good strains, high-count products, farmer trust and research backing over decades, not from one product launch.

manas.q: What were the keys to Brazil's soybean inoculant success?

children.note: A companion-planting system from icipe (Kenya) and Rothamsted (UK) that protects maize and sorghum from stemborers, striga weed and fall armyworm without pesticides.
Desmodium between maize rows repels stemborer moths (push); Napier or Brachiaria grass around the field attracts them (pull). Desmodium also draws in natural enemies.

manas.q: In push–pull, which plant pushes and which plant pulls the pests?

links.label: 📄 Source: Khan et al. 2014, Phil Trans R Soc B

children.note: Desmodium root chemicals cause suicidal germination and block striga attachment, while its shading and nitrogen fixation improve the soil.

links.label: 📄 Source: Khan et al. 2008, Field Crops Research

children.note: Farmers in 14 districts (2003–2006) had less stemborer damage, fewer striga plants and higher maize yields in push–pull plots than in maize alone.

links.label: 📄 Source: Khan et al. 2008, Field Crops Research

children.note: On 250 farms in Kenya, Uganda and Tanzania (2017), climate-adapted push–pull had about 83% fewer armyworm larvae and 2.7 times the maize yield of maize alone.

manas.q: How did climate-adapted push–pull affect fall armyworm and maize yield?

links.label: 📄 Source: Midega et al. 2018, Crop Protection

children.note: Desmodium and Napier/Brachiaria are good cattle fodder, so many push–pull farmers also gain milk income.

links.label: 📄 Source: Khan et al. 2014, Phil Trans R Soc B

children.note: Push–pull needs desmodium seed or vines, labour to establish and knowledge to manage. It suits mixed crop–livestock farms best.

A large research-for-development project (2009–2019, led by Wageningen University with African partners) that put legumes, inoculants and phosphorus into smallholder farms in about a dozen African countries.
Better legume varieties of soybean, beans, groundnut and cowpea; rhizobial inoculants; and phosphorus fertiliser, together with local inoculant production and testing.

children.topic: Key lesson: not every soil responds
children.note: Inoculants and legumes worked well on responsive soils but gave little on degraded 'non-responsive' soils lacking P, organic matter or other nutrients. Fix the soil first.

manas.q: What was a key N2Africa lesson about where inoculants work?

children.note: Kenya has one of Africa's most organised organic movements, serving both export and local markets.
The Kenya Organic Agriculture Network (KOAN) coordinates organic farming in Kenya: training, market links and certification support.

manas.q: Which organisation coordinates Kenya's organic sector?

children.topic: Kilimohai mark and East African standard

Sikkim decided in 2003 to go fully organic and completed the conversion by 2015–2016, becoming India's first fully organic state.

manas.q: When did Sikkim decide to go organic, and when was it declared fully organic?

children.note: Chemical inputs were phased out over more than a decade, with training, bio-villages, compost and certification support. Slowness was the key difference from Sri Lanka.

Supporters cite soil, health and tourism benefits; critics point to flat yields, dependence on food from other states and weak market premiums. Sikkim's farm area is small, so it is hard to copy at national scale.
Andhra Pradesh Community-managed Natural Farming (APCNF) is the world's largest state-backed agroecology programme, based on Zero Budget Natural Farming (ZBNF).
Farmer-to-farmer extension run by a state non-profit (RySS). Farmers use jeevamrit, beejamrit, mulching, multi-cropping and year-round green cover instead of synthetic inputs.
By 2020 about 523,000 farmers had converted roughly 13% of the state's farm area to ZBNF.

links.label: 📄 Source: Smith et al. 2020, Nature Sustainability

children.note: A 2025 study across the programme found ZBNF more than doubled farmers' profits, kept yields comparable and improved bird diversity.

manas.q: What did the 2025 Nature Ecology & Evolution study find about ZBNF profits and yields?

children.note: Controlled field trials in south-east India found natural-farming plots yielded more than conventional or organic plots, linked to better soil quality.
A 2020 analysis estimated natural farming can supply only 52–80% of the nitrogen normally applied as fertiliser, so higher-input farms may lose yield unless legumes fill the gap.

manas.q: What is the main scientific worry about scaling up zero budget natural farming?

links.label: 📄 Source: Smith et al. 2020, Nature Sustainability

children.note: A cluster-randomised trial (BLOOM) is testing whether APCNF improves diets and health of farming families.
Low-input farms can gain income with little yield loss; high-input farms need legumes and good transition plans. Evidence is improving but still debated.
In 2021 Sri Lanka tried to go 100% organic almost overnight. It is now the standard example of how NOT to make the transition.
In 2021 the government banned imports of chemical fertilisers and pesticides nationwide, aiming to become the first fully organic country.

manas.q: What did Sri Lanka do in 2021 that became a warning for organic transitions?

links.label: 📄 Source: Wikipedia, Economy of Sri Lanka

children.note: Tea and rice farmers reported large yield losses and higher costs; prices rose and protests followed. The ban was largely lifted in October–November 2021.

links.label: 📄 Source: Wikipedia, Economy of Sri Lanka

children.note: No transition period, not enough compost or bio-inputs available, little farmer training, and it came during an economic crisis.
Successful conversions (Sikkim, APCNF, Brazil inoculants) took 10+ years, built input supply and training first, and let farmers switch step by step.

manas.q: What is the main lesson from Sri Lanka's 2021 organic ban?

children.note: Governments and the UN now treat soil health as a policy goal, not just a farming detail.

Biologicals means biofertilisers, biopesticides and biostimulants. They are a fast-growing but still small part of farm-input sales.
Hundreds of promising agents (Bacillus, Trichoderma, Pseudomonas, Streptomyces, yeasts) are screened, but few become reliable products. Field consistency is the main hurdle.
Products need registration: PCPB (biopesticides) and KEPHIS in Kenya; FCO (biofertilisers) and CIB&RC (biopesticides) in India. Quality control builds trust, as Brazil showed.

children.note: Prove field results with trials, keep counts above label standards, train farmers, and market biologicals as part of a system, not a magic replacement.
